response:
ACCEPTThe four structural conclusions follow under the stated hypotheses and bundle definition. In particular, the square argument uses matching independence only across distinct blocks, the freezing criterion is exact for mixed as well as monochromatic bundles, and the first-entry argument gives an injection from block–color pairs into occupied-degree-four endpoints.The conclusion remains the stated structural reduction. The entry count supplies no donor assignment or improvement of a global grid bound. I treat the positive graft as the established illustration specified in your request; this review concerns the written mathematical arguments, not the implementation or reported enumeration.1. Hypotheses and the meaning of feasibilityThe initial perfect-matching existence assumption is present: since  $P$  is the endpoint set of a matching, that matching is a perfect matching of  $H=G[P]$ . Thus there is no missing existence hypothesis in the definitions of allowed edges or matching blocks.It is useful to make the bundle operation explicit. Fix a perfect matching  $N$ , and write  $m(x)$  for the matching mate of  $x$ . A set  $Q\subseteq P$  of promoted endpoints must satisfy
$$Q\cap m(Q)=\varnothing,$$
so that no matching edge contributes both endpoints. After promotion and deletion,
$$T'=T\cup Q,\qquad
P'=P\setminus\bigl(Q\cup m(Q)\bigr),\qquad
A'=A\setminus m(Q).$$
The unused edges of  $N$  give a perfect matching on  $P'$ .Since  $A'\subseteq A$ , every original selection remains feasible. Consequently, bundle feasibility reduces exactly to checking
$$\bigl|\Gamma_G(x)\cap A'\bigr|\le 1
\qquad(x\in Q).$$
The proof correctly uses  $d_A(p)\ge3$  as a hypothesis on the initial endpoint set. Your definition does not require all residual, unpromoted endpoints to retain occupied degree at least three after a bundle. This distinction matters for the validity of the constructed bundles, and the stated definition supports every use made in the note.The empty case is harmless: if  $P=\varnothing$ , the component statements are vacuous and  $f=j=0$ . Otherwise, finiteness supplies both the source/sink argument and termination of the freezing processes.2. Allowed edges, SCCs, and independent restrictionsThe matching facts in Section 2 are correct.Allowedness and directed cyclesFor the fixed matching  $N=\{b_iw_i\}$ , a directed cycle
$$i_1\longrightarrow i_2\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow i_k\longrightarrow i_1$$
expands into an  $N$ -alternating cycle: each arc represents a nonmatching edge  $b_{i_a}w_{i_{a+1}}$ , and the matching edges return from  $w_{i_{a+1}}$  to  $b_{i_{a+1}}$ . Flipping that alternating cycle gives a perfect matching containing every nonmatching edge on it.Conversely, if another perfect matching  $N'$  contains a nonmatching edge  $e$ , the component of  $N\triangle N'$  containing  $e$  is an alternating cycle. Under contraction, that cycle yields a directed cycle containing the arc corresponding to  $e$ .Therefore a nonmatching edge is allowed exactly when its arc lies on a directed cycle.SCCs are exactly the matching blocksAn arc lies on a directed cycle exactly when its endpoints belong to the same strongly connected component. Restoring the matching pairs therefore gives precisely the connected components of the allowed-edge graph:Every allowed nonmatching edge remains inside one restored SCC.The matching edges remain inside their own contracted vertices.A nontrivial SCC is connected through its internal arcs, so its restored allowed-edge graph is connected.In particular, every  $H$ -edge internal to one block is allowed. For a nonmatching edge this follows from strong connectivity; a matching edge is already allowed.A singleton SCC restores to a two-vertex block. Every perfect matching must use its single internal edge, so this is indeed a forced edge.Restriction and recombinationEvery edge used by any perfect matching is allowed by definition. Hence no perfect matching uses an edge between distinct matching blocks. Its restriction to every block is therefore a perfect matching of that block.Conversely, choosing one perfect matching separately in each block and taking their union gives a perfect matching of  $H$ . The blocks partition the vertices, so these choices have no vertex conflict.This proves exactly the independence used later. It does not assert simultaneous compatibility of arbitrary allowed edges within a single block.Finally, in a nontrivial SCC, each contracted vertex has an internal outgoing arc and an internal incoming arc. Together with its matching edge, these give:At least two allowed neighbors of its black endpoint.At least two allowed neighbors of its white endpoint.Thus every endpoint of a flexible block has at least two internal allowed neighbors. The stated block orientation is the SCC condensation orientation, so its acyclicity also follows.3. The square-unlocking proof is validThere are two compatibility issues here, and the proof handles both.The local geometry forces the displayed configurationIf a flexible endpoint  $p$  has at least two selected neighbors, its at least two allowed endpoint neighbors exhaust the other two grid directions. Thus it has exactly two  $P$ -neighbors and exactly two  $T$ -neighbors.Suppose its  $P$ -neighbors were opposite. Its two selected neighbors would then also be opposite. Each selected neighbor already has  $p$  as an occupied neighbor, so its other neighbors must be unoccupied. These restrictions make the two transverse neighbors of either  $P$ -neighbor unoccupied. That endpoint would have occupied degree at most two, contrary to the standing hypothesis.The perpendicular normalization in Section 3 is therefore valid.In the displayed coordinates, feasibility of the selections at  $(-1,0)$  and  $(0,-1)$  forces  $(-1,1)$  and  $(1,-1)$  blank. Hence the only possible occupied neighbors of  $q$  are  $p,s,v$ , and those of  $r$  are  $p,s,w$ . The lower degree bounds force all of them occupied and give
$$d_A(q)=d_A(r)=3.$$
The necessary vertices must exist in the ambient rectangle: a missing candidate neighbor would only make the degree contradiction stronger.Since  $s$  is adjacent to both occupied vertices  $q,r$ , it cannot be selected. Therefore  $s\in P$ .The argument placing  $s$  in  $C$  uses only legitimate independenceBoth  $pq$  and  $pr$  are allowed, because  $p$  has only those two endpoint neighbors and must have at least two allowed neighbors. Thus  $p,q,r$  lie in the same flexible block  $C$ .Assume  $s\notin C$ . Then  $qs$  and  $rs$  are disallowed. The possible endpoint neighbors of  $q$  are among  $p,s,v$ ; since  $q$  needs a second allowed neighbor besides  $p$ , it follows that
$$v\in P,\qquad qv\text{ is allowed},\qquad v\in C.$$
Likewise  $w\in C$  and  $rw$  is allowed.Now take a perfect matching  $N_0$ . It cannot match  $s$  to  $q$  or  $r$ , so it matches  $s$  to  $u$  or  $z$ .If  $su\in N_0$ , then  $u\notin C$ : matching edges remain within matching blocks. Choose a perfect matching whose restriction to  $C$  contains  $qv$ , and combine that restriction with  $N_0$  outside  $C$ . This gives one perfect matching containing both  $qv$  and  $su$ .The vertices  $q,v,u,s$  form a unit square. The alternative sides  $qs$  and  $vu$  are edges of  $H$ , since their endpoints belong to  $P$  and  $H$  is induced. The flip
$$\{qv,su\}\longmapsto\{qs,vu\}$$
therefore gives a perfect matching containing  $qs$ , contradicting its assumed disallowedness.If  $sz\in N_0$ , the same argument uses  $rw$  and the flip
$$\{rw,sz\}\longmapsto\{rs,wz\}.$$
Crucially, the two prescribed matching edges in either case lie in distinct blocks before recombination. There is no unproved within-block compatibility assumption.The final two-endpoint bundle is feasibleOnce  $s\in C$ , the internal edge  $qs$  is allowed. In any perfect matching containing  $qs$ , the vertex  $p$  must be matched to  $r$ , because its only endpoint neighbors are  $q,r$  and  $q$  is already matched.Thus this matching simultaneously contains  $qs$  and  $pr$ , for a direct degree reason.Promote  $q,r$  and delete their mates  $s,p$ . Their original occupied neighbor sets are
$$\Gamma_A(q)=\{p,s,v\},
\qquad
\Gamma_A(r)=\{p,s,w\}.$$
Each promoted vertex therefore retains exactly one occupied neighbor. Original selections remain feasible because occupancy only decreases.This establishes the claimed bundle of exactly two promoted endpoints. Consequently, exchange terminality implies that every flexible endpoint has at most one selected neighbor. The quantification over every perfect matching is essential here, and the note uses it correctly.4. Sources, sinks, and leaf geometryThe source/sink argument has the correct orientationLet  $C$  be a source block. Any edge from an external black endpoint to a white endpoint of  $C$  would be an incoming condensation edge. Hence every endpoint neighbor of a white endpoint of  $C$  lies inside  $C$ .Suppose  $C$  were flexible. By Section 3, each of its white endpoints has at most one selected neighbor. In any perfect matching, promote every white endpoint of  $C$  and delete its black mate. Since the matching restricts perfectly to  $C$ , this deletes all black endpoints of  $C$ , and hence all endpoint neighbors of the promoted vertices.Each promoted vertex retains at most one selected neighbor, giving a nonempty feasible bundle. This contradicts exchange terminality.Thus a source is a forced edge. Its white endpoint has no external endpoint neighbor and only its mate internally, so it is a  $P$ -leaf. Reversing colors gives the sink statement.Each nonempty connected component of  $H$  has a finite, nonempty condensation, with a source and a sink. No condensation edge connects different  $H$ -components. Consequently each endpoint component has a white  $P$ -leaf and a black  $P$ -leaf.The source and sink blocks may coincide when the component is a single forced edge; the claimed conclusion still holds.The exact leaf geometry also followsLet  $p$  be a  $P$ -leaf and  $q$  its sole endpoint neighbor. Since  $d_A(p)\ge3$ , it has at least two selected neighbors.If two selected neighbors were opposite, the same transverse-blank argument used in Section 3 would give  $d_A(q)\le2$ , a contradiction. Three selected neighbors contain an opposite pair, so that possibility is excluded as well.Therefore  $p$  has exactly two selected neighbors, they are perpendicular, and
$$d_A(p)=3.$$
Of these two selections, at least one is transverse to the edge  $pq$ . That selection forces a neighboring corner of  $q$  blank, giving  $d_A(q)\le3$ . Combined with the standing lower bound,
$$d_A(q)=3.$$
This argument covers all orientations and rectangular-boundary positions. It makes no assumption that an arbitrary leaf configuration lies strictly inside the rectangle.5. Freezing is an exact criterion, including mixed bundlesFix a matching  $N$ , a color  $c$ , and its mate map  $m$ .The freezing induction is validSuppose all previously frozen  $c$ -colored endpoints are excluded from every feasible  $c$ -colored bundle. If  $x$  has two neighbors in
$$T\cup m(E),$$
then each of those neighbors persists in every such bundle:An original selected vertex is never deleted.A vertex  $m(e)$ , with  $e\in E$ , can be deleted only by promoting  $e$ , which the induction hypothesis excludes.Thus both witnesses remain occupied, and  $x$  cannot be promoted.There is one small wording improvement available here. The induction proves “neither witness can be deleted,” whereas “their two witnesses cannot both be deleted” is literally weaker: retaining only one witness would not itself prevent promotion. The definitions and the stated induction supply the stronger assertion immediately, so this is a wording issue rather than a missing mathematical lemma.A nonempty fixed-point complement is a bundleAt a freezing fixed point, write
$$S=P_c\setminus E.$$
Because matching gives a bijection between the endpoint colors,
$$P_{\bar c}\setminus m(S)=m(E).$$
After promoting  $S$  and deleting  $m(S)$ , the occupied neighbors of any  $x\in S$  are therefore exactly
$$\Gamma_G(x)\cap\bigl(T\cup m(E)\bigr).$$
Same-color endpoints contribute no neighbors in a bipartite graph.Since the process is at a fixed point, this set has size at most one. Thus  $S$ , if nonempty, is a feasible monochromatic bundle. It automatically chooses at most one endpoint of each matching edge.Together with the induction, this proves:
$$\text{no feasible nonempty \(c\)-colored bundle}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{complete freezing in color \(c\)}.$$
Every nonempty color part of a mixed feasible bundle is feasibleLet  $Q$  be a mixed feasible bundle, and let  $Q_c$  be a nonempty color part. Passing from the full bundle to the sub-bundle  $Q_c$  changes occupancy from
$$A\setminus m(Q)
\quad\text{to}\quad
A\setminus m(Q_c).$$
The restored vertices are precisely  $m(Q\setminus Q_c)$ , all of which have color  $c$ . None is adjacent to a promoted vertex of  $Q_c$ . Thus the promoted vertices keep their feasible degrees.The vertices that cease to be promoted remain occupied, so their change of status introduces no additional occupied neighbor. Original selections remain feasible because the new occupied set is still a subset of  $A$ .Hence each nonempty color part of a mixed feasible bundle is feasible. Consequently,
$$\text{no nonempty bundle for \(N\)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{complete freezing in both colors}.$$
This closes the possible mixed-bundle gap.For precision, “any valid sequential freezing order” should be understood as an order continued to its fixed point. An arbitrarily truncated sequence need not yet have reached every block. Under exchange terminality, every such completed process freezes the entire color class: otherwise its fixed-point complement would be a bundle. No additional order-independence theorem is needed.6. The per-block, per-color first-entry argument proves  $2f\le j$ Fix one perfect matching and completed sequential freezing orders for both colors. Exchange terminality ensures both orders freeze all endpoints of their respective colors.Let  $x$  be the first frozen  $c$ -colored endpoint of a flexible block  $C$ , and let  $E$  be the endpoints frozen before  $x$ .No internal endpoint neighbor of  $x$  can belong to  $m(E)$ . Indeed, if  $y\in C\cap m(E)$ , then its mate  $m(y)$  belongs to  $C$ , because the matching restricts to  $C$ . Since  $y$  is adjacent to  $x$ , its mate has color  $c$ . Thus  $m(y)\in E\cap C$  would be an earlier frozen  $c$ -colored endpoint of  $C$ , contradicting the choice of  $x$ .Also, no selected vertex belongs to  $C$ , since  $C\subseteq P$ . Therefore all freezing witnesses for  $x$  are outside  $C$ .Now combine two disjoint lower bounds:Flexibility supplies at least two internal endpoint neighbors.Freezing supplies at least two outside persistent neighbors.The grid degree bound gives
$$4
\le
|\Gamma_G(x)\cap C|
+
\left|\Gamma_G(x)\cap\bigl(T\cup m(E)\bigr)\right|
\le d_A(x)\le4.$$
Every inequality is therefore an equality. In particular,  $x$  has:
$$\text{exactly two internal neighbors, exactly two outside witnesses, and }d_A(x)=4.$$
The outside witnesses cannot both be selected, by the square-unlocking consequence of Section 3. At least one is an endpoint in another block.The direction statement follows directly:For black  $x$ , an external endpoint witness is white, giving an outgoing edge from  $C$ .For white  $x$ , an external endpoint witness is black, giving an incoming edge to  $C$ .The count is an actual injectionFor each flexible block  $C$ , choose its first black entry and its first white entry in these fixed orders. Define
$$(C,c)\longmapsto x_{C,c}.$$
This map is injective:The two entries of one block have different colors.Entries from distinct blocks belong to disjoint vertex sets.Every image endpoint has occupied degree four. Hence
$$\boxed{2f\le j}.$$
The entries may depend on the matching and the freezing orders. The proof needs no canonical choice: one matching and one completed order per color supply the injection, while the local first-entry conclusion holds for every such choice.The degree-three corollary is valid in its stated special case. If every endpoint has occupied degree three, then  $j=0$ , hence  $f=0$ . All blocks are forced edges, which determines the matching uniquely. This remains consistent with exchange-terminal nonunique examples containing degree-four endpoints.The “first flexible entry globally” refinement is also correct. Before that entry, all frozen endpoints belong to forced blocks; their mates therefore belong to forced edges. Its two outside witnesses have precisely the two listed possible forms. Later entries can use mates of earlier frozen flexible endpoints, so the note correctly limits that refinement to the first global flexible entry.7. Resource accounting stays within what is provedSection 6 makes the appropriate distinctions.For a fixed tiling by four-vertex tiles, if  $k$  tiles contain all the occupied-degree-four endpoints, then
$$j\le4k,\qquad 2f\le j
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f\le2k.$$
This is a physical endpoint count. It establishes no payment assignment.Likewise, choosing one external endpoint witness for each entry gives exactly  $2f$  selected incidences. A physical cross-block edge has two endpoints, so it can receive at most two such incidences. The black and white freezing processes do not supply an argument reducing that upper bound to one. Thus the count does not establish an injection into distinct cross-block edges, forced matching edges, donors, or empty tiles.The note also correctly distinguishes an endpoint’s persistence in a freezing proof from the existence of a separate physical resource. The established positive graft can illustrate the coexistence of flexible matching structure and an existing payment, without making that payment available again.Accordingly, the remaining physical-tile ledger is a separate obligation. Nothing in the accepted structural proof resolves unrestricted compensation, general-grid equality, or a new global coefficient.
scope: Complete written flexible-block entry reduction only; two clarifications applied: BOTH witnesses persist, and sequential freezing orders are completed. No Python/Lean execution and no review of the later block tile ledger.
